title: Remembering Where You Came From
overview: Moses gives Israel two spoken rituals for life in the new land, one thanking God for the harvest by retelling their story and one promising they have shared their produce with the poor, then closes with a mutual pledge between God and the people.

parts.label: A basket of first produce (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Once settled, each farmer was to bring the earliest ripe crops of the year to the central place of worship, later understood to be Jerusalem. Handing them to the priest was a way of saying the land and its harvest were a gift from God, not simply their own achievement.

parts.label: Telling the family story (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: The "wandering Aramean" is most likely Jacob, who lived for years in Aram (roughly Syria) before his family went to Egypt; the Hebrew word can also mean close to dying. The worshiper retells a short history from homelessness and slavery to freedom and land, so that every harvest is tied to remembering a humble and painful past.

parts.label: A shared celebration (v. 11)
parts.note: The offering ended in a feast with the household, the Levites (the priestly tribe, who owned no farmland), and foreigners living among them. Thanks was meant to be shared with people who had no fields of their own.

parts.label: The third-year tithe (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: Every third year a tenth of the produce stayed in the home town and went to the Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows, the people with no land or family income. Because no priest checked this, the giver later declared out loud that he had handed it all over.

parts.label: An honest promise (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: The giver also declared he had not used this food while mourning or ritually unclean, states that kept a person away from holy things, nor given any "to the dead". Scholars are not sure exactly what that last phrase meant, but it probably refers to food offered in rites for the dead or to other gods.

parts.label: Both sides make a pledge (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Israel publicly declares that the LORD is their God and that they will follow his ways, and God declares them his own special people. It reads like a covenant (a binding agreement) being sealed on both sides, with Israel called to be set apart and honored among the nations.

think: What part of your own family's story, including the hard parts, do you think is worth retelling, and what would be lost if it were forgotten?
